body_markdown:
We spend a lot of energy trying to better manage our time. We plan our days, map out our to-do lists, and block off our calendars, all for the sake of squeezing a little more productivity out of the hours we have.


But what if time isn’t actually the problem?


Productivity expert and author[Maura Thomas](https://www.maurathomas.com/about-maura/) argues that the bigger challenge for today’s knowledge workers is managing their attention. We now work in an environment where email, Slack messages, notifications, meetings, and dozens of open tabs are constantly competing for our focus. Over time, that level of distraction has become so normal that we don’t even question it.


Maura has spent her career studying why traditional time management and discipline can’t help us get where we want to be. She sat down with RescueTime to talk about what it means to manage your attention, why willpower alone isn’t enough, and how both employees and leaders can create workdays that make focused work possible.


## Time management isn’t the problem anymore


Maura Thomas’s first job out of college was working for a company that sold planners. As she describes it, “I’ve been in the productivity space for my whole career.”


But as technology changed the way we worked, Maura started to question if traditional time management was still the right framework. Once the iPhone became mainstream and constant connectivity became part of everyday life, she started seeing a different problem emerge. People didn’t need more hours or better calendars. They needed a better way to protect where their attention went.


Now, this TEDx speaker and author of[Attention Management](https://www.maurathomas.com/books/attention-management-book/) ** and[Everyone Wants to Work Here](https://www.maurathomas.com/books/everyone-wants-to-work-here/) teaches others that the path to productivity isn’t so much about managing your time as it is about managing your attention.


“Our biggest challenge is not that we don’t have enough time. If you’ve ever had a day where you thought to yourself, that was such a good day, I got so much done. Then, in theory, we all have the time that we need to have productive days. So, it’s not really that time is the obstacle. I think now the obstacle is that we have too many distractions.”


Our digital tools are constantly competing for our attention, but[it’s what they were designed to do](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/the-digital-self/202401/technologys-original-sin-is-the-theft-of-attention) . So when we view distraction as poor time management, the solution involves more discipline or more hours.


Maura argues that these approaches don’t fully address the environment that knowledge workers are operating in. In what she calls the[‘attention economy](https://www.maurathomas.com/how-dopamine-keeps-you-scrolling/) ,’ attention itself has become something other people and platforms are constantly trying to capture. To be truly productive, then, you need to start with recognizing that competition and becoming more intentional about what gets your attention in the first place.


## We’ve normalized a distracted way of working


Research from Microsoft[estimates](https://news.microsoft.com/de-ch/2025/06/17/new-microsoft-study-reveals-the-rise-of-the-infinite-workday-40-of-employees-check-email-before-6-a-m-evening-meetings-up-16/) that the average employee receives 117 emails and 153 Teams messages each day. It wasn’t always this way, though. The volume of interruptions and accompanying expectations grew gradually, in what Maura describes as the “boiling frog”:


“It just keeps ratcheting up and ratcheting up and ratcheting up until I think that we’ve sort of collectively thrown up our hands and said, ‘I guess this is just the way it is. I’m so stressed all the time, I’m always behind, I always leave work thinking I was busy all day, and I got nothing done.’ We think we just have to work harder, which for most people means more hours. And so, we keep working more hours, and then we’re checking our messages at the dinner table and from the soccer field, and we’re caught up in this constant grind, constant connectivity.”


The irony is that many of us now arrange our work around distraction. **“The attention economy has convinced us that distraction is the norm,”** Maura says. “Distraction is just our constant companion in everyday life.”


But normal doesn’t mean inevitable. Maura argues that recognizing how much our environment competes for our attention is an important first step toward reclaiming some control over it. After all, we aren’t dealing with an occasional interruption or a lack of self-discipline. We’re operating in a world where attention has value.


“The world is engineered, our environment is engineered to keep us distracted,” she says. “Willpower alone isn’t enough, so **it’s** **really important to recognize how our attention is being harvested for profit** .”


## Stop expecting willpower to protect your attention


Since distraction is built into our environment, just trying harder to ignore it isn’t a particularly effective strategy.


“Discipline, I suppose, depending on how you define it, is certainly important,” Maura says. We need to do the things we need to do. But it’s very hard to have discipline without awareness and motivation.”


Awareness comes first. Before you can protect your attention, you have to notice what keeps pulling it away. It might be the email tab you leave open all day or the phone sitting within reach every time you get stuck. If you use RescueTime, you can access a report that details which apps and tools are stealing your attention.


Once you start noticing those distractions, you can change the conditions that make them so easy to give in. Close your inbox while you’re writing or put your phone out of your reach while you work.


In other words, don’t repeatedly ask yourself to resist a distraction you could remove instead.


## Separate proactive work from reactive work


When Maura is working with a client, she typically introduces them to the ‘ *between, not during* ’ rule. When you decide you’re going to take on a task, whether it’s writing an article, working on a spreadsheet, or performing some research, you close your communication channels and just do the thing.


“Check your communication as often as you feel like you need to, *but do it in between other things* instead of during other things,” Maura says. “The research shows that when we are task switching, everything we do takes longer, and the quality is lower.​”


You don’t have to completely avoid your notifications and stop communicating with your colleagues. You just need to stop replying to messages when your focus is honed in on another task. One solution is to try a modified[Pomodoro](https://blog.rescuetime.com/pomodoro-method-for-productivity/) . Work for 25 minutes, check your communication, then take a 5-minute break.


RescueTime’s Focus Sessions can help reinforce that boundary. When you’re ready to work on something that requires your full attention, start a Focus Session to block distracting websites and apps for a set period of time. The end of the session becomes your time to check messages, respond to what needs your attention, and then move intentionally in your next block of work.


Reactive work is an expected part of any job. Giving it its own time keeps it from infringing on your proactive work tasks.


## Attention management requires the right workplace culture


Up to this point, most of these strategies put the individual in control. But when you’re working on a team, there’s a limit to how much you can accomplish when the company culture rewards the opposite behavior.


“If people understand how to manage their attention and they do all the right things—check between not during, they use RescueTime, they understand that they have to close their email so that they can do thoughtful work—but if the culture that they work in doesn’t support those best practices, then it’s never going to work,” Maura says. “It’s like Sisyphus pushing the rock up the hill. Eventually, you’re just going to say ‘never mind.’”


That doesn’t mean employees have no responsibility for their own focus. In fact, Maura argues that ultimately, no one else can protect your attention for you. But[leaders are responsible](https://www.maurathomas.com/how-corporate-culture-affects-productivity/) for creating a workplace where protecting it is actually possible.


“I wouldn’t say that it’s a leader’s job to take responsibility for someone else’s attention,” she says. “But I do think a leader’s job is to specifically engineer a culture of productivity instead of a culture of urgency.”


A culture of urgency treats everything like it needs an immediate response. Fast = good,[visible = productive](https://blog.rescuetime.com/being-seen-vs-being-effective/) . Like the constant distractions we’ve gotten used to, Maura believes that this culture develops gradually rather than through intentional decision.


She suggests that leaders ask, “How can we respond to our customers and our prospects in a way that we think is necessary without undermining our team’s ability to be productive?”


Protecting attention, then, requires both sides. Employees need to take control of where their attention goes, while leaders need to stop creating environments that constantly pull it away.


## Treat communication like part of your infrastructure


One key place leaders can start is by looking at how information moves through their organization.


“Communication is really the assembly line of knowledge work,” Maura asserts. She compares our current age of knowledge work to the industrial age. “Assembly lines and the accompanying processes were engineered to be as specific and efficient as possible. Great attention was paid to: *How do we design this machine* ? *How do the people work the machines to drive the greatest amount of efficiency and therefore profit* ?”


Knowledge work produces different things: ideas, analysis, solutions, creativity, and innovation. Maura suggests that the systems supporting that work deserve the same level of attention.


Instead, workplace communication is often left largely up to personal preference. “Everybody tells everybody whatever they think they need to know in whatever format they prefer,” she says, whether that’s chat, text, a CRM, a voicemail, or an in-person meeting. “ **It is completely chaotic** .”


She paints this picture: “Can you imagine if, in the Industrial Age, the floor supervisor gathered all the staff together and said, ‘Alright, everybody, just jump on some machine, find something you like, just go ahead and do whatever you want, and I’m sure the products will get made. That wouldn’t have happened, and yet that’s how we’re treating communication now.”


Two changes can help reshape workplace communication and improve the employee experience.


First, make information transparent and accessible. Employees shouldn’t have to ask anyone to get the information they need to do their job. Organizations can intentionally decide where information lives and how employees are expected to access it.


Second, establish communication policies. Instead of letting everyone decide individually whether something belongs in an email, chat, meeting, text, or another tool, define which channels should be used for which situations.


[Engineer communication](https://www.maurathomas.com/corporate-communication-strategies/) with the same precision as your other business systems. It makes it infinitely easier for employees to get the information they need without interruption.


## Make the way you work more intentional


Many of us already have a productivity system, but it’s not always one we put a lot of thought into.


“Most people work through a collection of habits,” Maura says, mentioning habits like written lists, sticky notes, flagged emails, and appointments with ourselves. These habits tend to accumulate over time as we find new ways to keep up with everything competing for our attention.


Instead of just adding new habits when work starts feeling unmanageable, however, Maura encourages people to take a step back and[look at the system](https://www.maurathomas.com/how-to-stay-organized-at-work-a-systems-approach/) as a whole. She breaks it into six areas: attention management, task management, communication, work-life balance, habits, and culture and environment. Her[Empowered Productivity Assessment](https://www.maurathomas.com/productivity-assessment/) is designed to help identify where those systems may be working well, or working against you.


The goal isn’t to optimize every part of your day until you somehow manage to fit everything in. As Maura points out, “no matter how organized and how productive you are, too much is still too much.”


Instead, being more intentional about how you work can help you make better decisions about what gets your limited attention in the first place. After all, the goal of attention management isn’t to triple your output. It’s to make sure that the things that matter most aren’t overshadowed by whatever happens to demand your attention first.


That’s also why the familiar feeling of *I was busy all day, but I got nothing done* can be so frustrating. Usually, it isn’t quite true. We did plenty. As Maura explains, “It just wasn’t the things that mattered the most to us.”


Learning how to manage your attention is what helps you close the gap between what fills your day and what you actually want to happen during the day.
